chapters.title: Chapter 3: Case Studies in Currency Wars

lessons.title: China's Yuan Management: From Peg to Managed Float

body.text: China has been on both sides of the currency war argument within a single decade: accused of undervaluing the yuan for years, then forced to spend nearly a trillion dollars of reserves defending it from falling too far. The full history is far messier than either accusation alone suggests.

children.text: Before 1994, China ran two exchange rates at once: an official rate of roughly 5.8 yuan per dollar used for state transactions, and a much weaker secondary swap-market rate of roughly 8.7 yuan per dollar that reflected the currency's real market value for most actual trade. On 1 January 1994, China unified the two rates at the weaker, market-reflective level, an active, one-off devaluation of the official rate that predates every other China currency episode in this course.

body.title: Measure the 1994 Move
body.prompt: The official rate moved from about 5.8 yuan per dollar to about 8.7 yuan per dollar. By what percentage did the yuan-per-dollar rate increase? (This is one common convention used to describe this devaluation's size.)
body.explanation: (8.7 − 5.8) / 5.8 ≈ 50%. Note the convention matters here: measured the other way, the yuan's dollar value fell from 1/5.8 to 1/8.7, a drop of about 33%. Both '50% devaluation' and '33% devaluation' appear in different sources describing this exact same 1994 move, purely because of which rate is used as the base. Always check which convention a cited devaluation percentage is using before comparing it across sources.

children.text: Pegged, Then Floating, Then Re-Pegged: 1994 to 2010

markDefs.definition: The official daily reference rate the PBoC sets for the yuan against the dollar, around which the currency is allowed to trade within a specified band (widened over time, currently ±2%) each day.

children.text: After 1994, China held the yuan tightly pegged near 8.28 to the dollar for over a decade, a period when US officials began arguing the currency was being kept deliberately undervalued to support exports. In July 2005, China shifted to a managed float referencing a basket of currencies, letting the yuan appreciate gradually to around 6.83 by mid-2008. The mechanism China uses to manage this, then and now, is the
, set by the PBoC each morning, with actual trading allowed within a band around it.

That gradual appreciation stopped the moment the 2008 financial crisis hit. China re-pegged the yuan tightly to the dollar around 6.83 to shield its exporters during the crisis, only resuming managed appreciation in June 2010 under sustained G20 pressure, the exact episode referenced in the 2010 currency war lesson earlier in this course.

events.title: Dual rates unified
events.description: China unifies its official and swap-market exchange rates, an active devaluation of the official rate to around 8.7 yuan per dollar.

events.title: Tight dollar peg
events.description: The yuan holds near 8.28 to the dollar for over a decade, drawing sustained US accusations of deliberate undervaluation.

events.title: Managed float begins
events.description: China moves off the strict dollar peg toward a basket-referenced managed float, allowing gradual appreciation to around 6.83 by mid-2008.

events.title: Re-pegged during the financial crisis
events.description: Appreciation is paused and the yuan is held near 6.83 to protect exporters through the global financial crisis.

events.title: Managed appreciation resumes
events.description: Under G20 pressure, China resumes gradual yuan appreciation, the backdrop to the 2010 currency war era covered earlier in this course.

children.text: You already met this episode in Chapter 1: the PBoC's cumulative near-3% cut to the yuan's daily reference rate over 11 to 13 August 2015, framed officially as a technical reform to make the fixing more market-driven, and read globally as the opening move of a fresh currency war. What that earlier lesson didn't cover is what happened next, and it complicates the simple devaluation story considerably.

The August 2015 move triggered exactly the kind of capital flight a genuinely weaker, less controlled yuan invites. Rather than letting the currency keep sliding, the PBoC spent enormous reserves over the following eighteen months buying yuan and selling dollars to slow the depreciation, the opposite action of a country chasing a competitive devaluation.

stats.context: The high point before the defense phase began

stats.label: China's forex reserves, early 2017
stats.context: After roughly $1 trillion was spent defending the yuan from capital outflow pressure

body.text: This is the nuance a simple 'China devalues its currency for export advantage' headline misses entirely. For roughly two years after August 2015, the PBoC was fighting to keep the yuan from falling further, not pushing it down. A government that manages its currency actively can end up defending either side of the market depending on the year, sometimes within the same decade, which is exactly why this course keeps insisting on checking the actual mechanism and motive rather than trusting the headline label.

children.text: 2019 to 2020: The Manipulator Label, Finally Applied

markDefs.definition: A formal US Treasury determination that a trading partner is deliberately manipulating its currency for unfair trade advantage, carrying potential trade consequences under US law.

children.text: Chapter 1 mentioned the US repeatedly threatened, but never applied, a formal

against China during the 2010 era. That changed on 5 August 2019, in the middle of the US-China trade war, when the yuan weakened past the psychologically significant level of 7 per dollar for the first time since the global financial crisis, and the US Treasury formally labelled China a currency manipulator, its first such designation of any country since 1994, the same year as the devaluation that opened this lesson. The label was removed in January 2020 as part of the Phase One trade agreement between the two countries.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Phase Is This?
body.question: Between late 2015 and 2017, the PBoC spent roughly a trillion dollars of reserves buying yuan and selling dollars. What was it trying to achieve?
options: Push the yuan lower to boost export competitiveness
Slow the yuan's depreciation and stem capital flight, the opposite of a competitive devaluation
Prepare for a return to the 1994 dual-rate system
Comply with a binding IMF instruction to weaken the currency
body.explanation: This was defensive intervention against depreciation, not an attempt to engineer one. It is the clearest evidence in the yuan's history that China's currency management cannot be reduced to a single, permanent 'keep it weak' strategy: the direction of intervention has flipped multiple times depending on what pressure the currency was actually under.

body.title: The Two Faces of Yuan Management

columns.label: Weakening phases
points: 1994 unification, 1994-2005 tight peg, August 2015 reference-rate cut
Motive: protect or boost export competitiveness
Drew undervaluation accusations from trading partners
Reserves generally build during these periods

columns.label: Defending phases
points: 2015-2017 post-shock intervention, occasional periods of yuan strength management
Motive: prevent disorderly depreciation and capital flight
Rarely makes headlines the way a devaluation does
Reserves are spent down heavily during these periods

body.title: You Are Reading a Headline About the Yuan
body.scenario: A financial news alert says: 'Yuan weakens past key level as PBoC sets lower daily fixing, reviving currency war fears.' You want to assess whether this is a genuine competitive devaluation signal or something else, using only what this lesson has taught you about how to read PBoC actions.
body.prompt: What three things would you check before concluding this is a deliberate, export-motivated devaluation?
body.modelAnswer: First, check the size and persistence of the fixing change: a single day's modest move within the normal trading band is very different from a sustained multi-day cut like August 2015. Second, check what China's reserves are doing around the same time: rising reserves alongside yuan weakness suggests a genuine, tolerated depreciation, while falling reserves suggest the PBoC may actually be fighting the move rather than causing it. Third, check the broader context: is this happening during a period of trade tension, capital outflow pressure, or a global risk-off event, any of which could explain currency weakness with no export-competitiveness motive at all. A headline alone, without these three checks, tells you almost nothing about whether this is the offensive devaluation the phrase 'currency war' implies.

cards.definition: The PBoC's daily reference rate for the yuan against the dollar, around which trading is allowed within a set band.
China's active devaluation that merged its official and swap-market exchange rates into a single, weaker rate on 1 January 1994.
A formal US Treasury finding of deliberate currency manipulation, applied to China briefly from August 2019 to January 2020, its first use since 1994.
A central bank spending reserves to slow a currency's depreciation, the opposite action of a competitive devaluation, as China did from 2015 to 2017.

points: China's own history includes a genuine active devaluation, the January 1994 unification of its dual exchange rates, predating every other China episode covered in this course.
The yuan moved from a tight dollar peg (1994-2005) to a managed float (from 2005), with a crisis-driven re-peg in 2008-2010, showing the regime itself has changed multiple times.

After the August 2015 reference-rate cut, China spent roughly a trillion dollars of reserves over the following two years defending the yuan from falling further, the opposite of a competitive devaluation.

The US Treasury's currency manipulator label was finally applied to China in August 2019 during the trade war, and removed in January 2020 as part of a trade agreement, its first use of the designation since 1994.
Reducing China's currency management to a single permanent 'keeps the yuan weak' narrative misses that the PBoC has actively defended both directions at different points in the same decade.
The next lesson turns to Japan, where the yen and the global carry trade tell a different but related story about currency intervention and its risks.
